At least four dispatchers a shift, around the clock, per Milwaukee Magazine. Roughly 105,000 routine calls a year, per the county. Cory Lynch, the operations supervisor, says being a 24/7 department made them the default for anything to do with municipalities or police departments.

"Then we have to put that caller on hold to answer a 911 call that could be for an accident, and then picking the caller back up and having them start their story over again if it happens to be another dispatcher that answers it."

La Crosse bought it from a Seattle company called Aurelian. Every step above was drawn by a person before the phone ever rang. That is a workflow, rung 4 of five, and for this job rung 4 is the right answer. The vendor calls it an agent.

If somebody in trouble calls the routine line, the system picks up certain hot words and sends them to a 911 dispatcher, per the county's operations supervisor. That list is not something the model worked out. Somebody sat down and typed it. The machine is matching words, not judging urgency.

About 65 percent of the calls the system took never reached a dispatcher, per the county's own count. That counts calls that ended, not calls that got answered. No resolution or complaint figure exists on any page we fetched, including the vendor's own.
COUNTY'S OWN COUNT, REPORTED BY NEWS 8000
The same product went sideways at another Wisconsin desk

Ozaukee County bought the same product and went live around the clock in week one. Callers asked for a sheriff when they meant a deputy. Shouting and music confused it. They cut it back to two hours a day while the vendor worked through it, and the sheriff says the vendor has been receptive.

About $67,000 in year one and about $81,000 in year two, per Milwaukee Magazine, priced on call volume. That is not a price rise. That is the product working harder, invoiced. Milwaukee Magazine put the annual price at about one employee with benefits. If your calls triple in July, model your July.

Never point it where a wrong route costs a house or a hand. A caller here says a village name or a mile marker, which is a harder version of what broke Ozaukee. Test that before you sign. Under a few thousand routine calls a year, the honest answer is a better phone tree and an online payment page.
